newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenya opposition may have stiffened Moi's resistance.
newsitem.headline: Kenya opposition may have stiffened Moi's resistance.

text.p: Kenya's opposition believes its protest on "budget day" was a spectacular success but the punch-up in parliament is likely to stiffen President Daniel arap Moi's resistance to reforms.
Diplomats who had ringside seats at Thursday's fisticuffs said the 73-year-old leader was even less likely to offer concessions after the televised assault on his dignity.
"The expression on Moi's face as he watched the scenes ranged from 'This is tedious children's stuff' to 'I am getting really irritated'," one senior Western envoy in Nairobi said.
"I imagine he's pretty seething inside and what happened will confirm his view that these (opposition) people are not fit to run a railroad," he said.
The usually divided opposition has found a fragile cohesion in its campaign to win sweeping changes to the constitution before elections due this year.
Prevented by a thick security blanket from demonstrating in the streets, the opposition picked a natural theatre -- the chamber of the national assembly -- to make its point.

Shouting and stamping, opposition members of parliament (MPs) prevented Finance Minister Musalia Mudavadi from audibly reading his budget speech. As the tension rose, jostling and fights broke out on the floor.
Moi was present and state television, which is tightly controlled, broadcast some of the chaos live before transmission was abruptly halted.
The opposition viewed the disruption, and by extension the public show of disrespect to Moi, as a triumph.
"The minister read his speech but nobody heard him at all. We managed to disrupt him and so our campaign was very successful," Raila Odinga, an opposition leader, said later.
The presidency was silent on Friday but an editorial in the ruling party's newspaper denounced the protest in parliament as "horrendous".
"Changes will not be forced on the government. dialogue and civilised discourse are more likely to help solve the impasse," the Kenya Times said.
The space for such dialogue is shrinking rapidly.
The opposition has the tacit support of many donors led by the United States when it says the constitution and electoral laws are flawed by repressive or pro-regime provisions.
With public backing from church leaders and most of civic society, the opposition says the elections cannot be fair without wholesale reforms which Moi has already rejected.
But the donors are not applying anything like maximum pressure on Moi. Most say the main opposition leaders have a credibility problem because of their tribal constituencies.
They also fear the spread of more upheaval in Africa to a country which remains a commercial and diplomatic hub.
Astutely, Moi has not asked for a cent of donor money to fund the elections, restricting outsiders' right to interfere in the way they are run.
Yet the potential threat of a boycott hangs over the polls whose date Moi has not yet announced.
More immediately the opposition needs to prove it has popular support among 30 million Kenyans for its cause.
"So far there is no overwhelming evidence that ordinary people are very excited about what are rather abstract calls for constitutional change," one Western ambassador in Nairobi said.
To manifest the support it claims, the opposition has to defy almost routine bans on public rallies and run the risk of escalating violence.
Only a few hundred students took that risk on Thursday and challenged the heavy police and paramilitary presence on the semi-deserted streets of the capital.
A cycle of political clashes, reminiscent of the torrid election period in 1992, will test the level of genuine opposition support among those with most to lose -- Nairobi's middle classes.

The country's leading newspaper, the Daily Nation, moved from its usual broad support for the opposition on Friday. Voicing the case for dialogue and moderation, it challenged the claim that Thursday's punch-up was positive.

"City residents did not stay away from work because they are against reforms; but because they are against the methods being adopted by the reform lobby, which seeks confrontation. They are also upset with the government that refuses to listen to its citizens. This simply can't go on," the Nation said in an editorial.
